text: Once you've picked a paper, the real work begins: turning its prose, figures, and equations into a concrete, buildable plan — the circuit, the parameters, the comparison — before you write a single line of code.

This lesson covers a systematic process for extracting a methodology from text, figures, and equations, how to handle the near-universal gap between what a paper describes and what it actually specifies, where papers bury the details you need, and how to write your own methodology document before coding.

Identify the exact result you're targeting — one figure, one table row, not the paper's overall finding. Trace that result backward through methods to find what circuit and parameters produce it. Check every figure caption and table footnote, since papers routinely put essential values there, not just in the body text. Check the appendix for anything the main text references but doesn't fully specify, and check cited prior work the paper builds on without re-explaining. Then write your own methodology document, in your own words, distinct from the paper's — this step is where you discover what you actually don't understand yet, before it costs you debugging time.

Even well-written papers rarely specify every detail needed for an exact rebuild. Your job is distinguishing details that plausibly don't affect the qualitative result — like a stochastic optimizer's exact random seed, reasonable to choose yourself and document — from details that plausibly do affect the result and aren't specified, like which specific error-mitigation sub-technique was used when several variants exist. That second kind is a real gap you must flag explicitly, not silently guess around, because it directly affects how you'd interpret a discrepancy later.

In a worked example, a paper states it prepared a three-qubit GHZ state and applied zero-noise extrapolation, executing 1,024 shots per noise-scaling factor. A figure caption adds the scaling factors: one, one point five, two, two point five, and three. The appendix states Richardson extrapolation was used. Extracting this: the circuit is a standard GHZ preparation you already know how to build, the technique is unitary folding per a cited method you'd need to pull up, and the gap you'd flag is that the paper never states the extrapolation's exact fitting tolerance — your own reasonable choice, not the paper's specification.
Next lesson covers what happens when you run your extracted methodology and your numbers don't match the paper's — the single most common outcome of a real reproduction attempt.
